sentences.text: The generic name Asiatosuchus translates to "Asian crocodile", reflecting its geographic origins.
Species within this genus possessed a generalized crocodilian form featuring flat, triangular skulls when viewed from above.
Their upper jaw teeth completely overlapped the lower jaw teeth, creating a distinct overbite.
The species A. depressifrons can be distinguished from others by a large hole and depression in the jugal bone.
Based on largely complete skeletons, A. grangeri may have reached 4 meters in length, while A. germanicus is estimated to have grown to 6.5 meters.
The genus Asiatosuchus was established by paleontologist Charles Mook in 1940, who also named the type species A. grangeri that same year.
The species now known as A. depressifrons was first named in 1855 under the name Crocodilus depressifrons.
In 1964, Chinese paleontologist Yang Zhongjian named A. nanlingensis based on fragmentary material from the Shanghu Formation in Guangdong, China.
Well-preserved remains from Germany and France were described in 1966 and assigned to the new species A. germanicus.
Two additional species were named from Russia: A. zajsanicus in 1982 and A. volgensis in 1993.
The presence of Asiatosuchus in marine deposits suggests these crocodilians could tolerate prolonged time in the ocean, aiding their dispersal across Europe and Asia.
Small fossilized coprolites, or feces, were found alongside the specimen of A. nanlingensis.
Phylogenetic analyses classify Asiatosuchus as a basal member of the evolutionary group Crocodyloidea, near the split from Alligatoroidea.
A 2021 morphological study determined that A. nanlingensis is the sister taxon of Kambara murgonensis within the subfamily Mekosuchinae, and most analyses find the genus is paraphyletic.
This extinct genus of crocoid inhabited Eurasia during the Paleogene, living from the Selandian to the Priabonian stages between 60.9 and 33.9 million years ago.
German remains of A. germanicus originated from the Messel Pit quarry, a site preserving life from Eocene anoxic lakes and subtropical forests.
A Pakistani fossil was found in the Middle Eocene Drazinda Formation, a marine deposit that also preserved archaeocete whale remains.
Recent studies suggest that only the species A. grangeri belongs in the genus Asiatosuchus.
It is debated whether A. nanlingensis and Eoalligator chunyii are synonymous, though a 2016 analysis proposed they were synonyms while a 2017 article disputed this, treating them as distinct species.

A. volgensis and A. zajsanicus were regarded as nomina dubia because they are based on specimens with very little preserved anatomical detail, a view shared by Angielczyk and Gingerich in 1998 due to poor preservation.
